title: Lesson 2: Understanding the Difference Between Disagreement and Disrespect
summary: Disagreement is a different opinion. Disrespect is treating someone without regard for their dignity. Express differences professionally without attacking the person.

items.label: Duration
items.body: 45–60 minutes

items.label: Participants
items.body: All Zura Spa staff

items.label: Focus
items.body: Respectful communication, emotional intelligence, professional boundaries and conflict prevention

sections.title: 1. Introduction
paragraphs: Imagine two therapists working at Zura Spa.
One therapist believes that treatment rooms should be prepared immediately after each massage session.
Another therapist believes that the rooms should also be checked shortly before the next appointment.
The first therapist says: "I think preparing everything immediately after each session will help us avoid delays."
The second therapist responds: "I understand your point, but I think checking again before the next appointment is also important."
Both employees have different opinions, but they are communicating respectfully.
This is disagreement.
Now imagine the conversation takes a different direction.
The first therapist says: "Your suggestion doesn't make sense. You clearly don't know how to organise your work."
The second responds: "Who are you to tell me what to do? You think you're better than everybody!"
The discussion becomes heated.
What began as a difference of opinion has turned into disrespect.
The important lesson is that the employees did not become disrespectful because they disagreed. They became disrespectful because of how they expressed their disagreement.
Disagreement means having a different opinion. Disrespect means treating another person inappropriately or without regard for their dignity.
At Zura Spa, employees do not have to agree on everything. However, they must learn to express their differences professionally.

sections.title: 2. What is disagreement?
paragraphs: Disagreement occurs when two or more people have different opinions, ideas, preferences or interpretations of a situation.
Disagreement is normal in a workplace because employees have different experiences, personalities and ways of thinking.
These situations are not automatically disrespectful.
You can disagree with someone's opinion while still respecting that person.
Respect does not require everyone to think alike.

sections.title: Examples at Zura Spa
list: Two therapists suggest different approaches to preparing treatment rooms.
A receptionist and therapist have different opinions about scheduling appointments.
An employee believes a task should be completed differently.
A supervisor and employee interpret an instruction differently.
Staff members suggest different ways to improve client service.

sections.title: 3. What is disrespect?
paragraphs: Disrespect occurs when someone communicates or behaves in a way that disregards another person's dignity, legitimate boundaries or right to professional treatment.
A receptionist suggests changing the arrangement of certain administrative tasks.
Another employee responds: "Nobody asked for your opinion. Just keep quiet."
The problem is not that the employee disagrees.
The problem is that she dismisses her colleague disrespectfully.
Better response: "I understand your suggestion, but I think the current arrangement may work better because it allows us to confirm appointments earlier."
The employee has expressed disagreement without attacking the other person.
list: Insulting someone.
Mocking their opinions.
Shouting to intimidate them.
Making degrading comments.
Deliberately humiliating them.
Repeatedly interrupting to silence them.
Using offensive sarcasm.
Threatening someone.
Dismissing them because of their position.
Retaliating because they expressed a different opinion.

sections.title: 4. Key differences between disagreement and disrespect
paragraphs: Disagreement: "I don't think that approach will work because it may delay the next appointment."
Disrespect: "That is a stupid idea. You clearly don't know what you're doing."
The first statement challenges an idea.
The second attacks the person expressing it.
Challenge the idea without attacking the individual.
table: Often involves hostility or degrading behaviour

sections.title: 5. Why disagreement is normal and sometimes beneficial
paragraphs: Disagreement should not automatically be treated as a workplace problem.
When managed appropriately, different perspectives can help a team make better decisions.

sections.title: 1. It introduces different ideas
paragraphs: Employees may suggest improvements that others have not considered.

sections.title: 2. It helps identify problems
paragraphs: A respectful disagreement may reveal weaknesses in an existing process.

sections.title: 3. It encourages clearer communication
paragraphs: Employees learn to explain their reasoning and ask relevant questions.

sections.title: 4. It strengthens teamwork
paragraphs: Teams develop mutual understanding by discussing differences constructively.

sections.title: 5. It develops professional maturity
paragraphs: Employees learn that another person's different opinion does not automatically threaten their own value.

sections.title: 6. Why employees sometimes interpret disagreement as disrespect
paragraphs: Sometimes an employee feels disrespected simply because another person does not agree with her.
A supervisor suggests a new way of arranging appointments.
A receptionist says: "I understand the idea, but I'm concerned it may create overlapping bookings. Could we review how it would work?"
This is not automatically disrespectful.
The receptionist is raising a practical concern.
A respectful question is not the same as insubordination, and a different opinion is not automatically a personal attack.

items.label: Personal pride
items.body: The employee believes her opinion should always be accepted.

items.label: Emotional sensitivity
items.body: A different opinion feels like rejection.

items.label: Misunderstanding
items.body: The employee interprets a direct response as hostility.

items.label: Fear of losing authority
items.body: A supervisor believes that questions or alternative suggestions automatically challenge leadership.

items.label: Previous experiences
items.body: Past humiliation influences how the employee interprets current conversations.

items.label: Existing tension
items.body: An employee interprets neutral statements negatively because of an earlier disagreement.

sections.title: 7. Disagreeing with colleagues respectfully
paragraphs: Employees should be able to express different opinions without damaging workplace relationships.
A therapist says: "I think we should prepare all supplies at the beginning of the shift."

Another therapist responds: "I understand your suggestion. However, some supplies may need replenishing after individual sessions. Perhaps we should combine an opening check with a post-session check."
This response demonstrates three important habits: acknowledging the colleague's suggestion, explaining a different perspective, and proposing a practical solution.
Employees should avoid turning a difference of opinion into a competition over who is superior.
list: "I understand your point, but I see it differently."
"Could we consider another approach?"
"My understanding is slightly different."
"I agree with part of what you're saying."
"Can we review the facts before deciding?"
"I think there may be a better way to handle this."

sections.title: 8. Disagreeing with a supervisor respectfully
paragraphs: Employees may sometimes have concerns about instructions, decisions or procedures.
Respecting a supervisor does not mean employees must pretend to agree with everything.
However, disagreements should be communicated professionally.
A supervisor asks a receptionist to move an appointment to a different time.
The receptionist notices that the proposed time conflicts with another confirmed booking.
Disrespectful response: "That doesn't make sense. You clearly don't understand the schedule."
Professional response: "I understand the proposed change. However, there's already a confirmed appointment at that time. Could we review the schedule before making the adjustment?"
The employee has identified a potential problem without insulting the supervisor.

Where an instruction raises an immediate safety or consent concern, the employee should not proceed with unsafe conduct merely to avoid disagreement. The concern should be raised promptly through an appropriate channel.

sections.title: Important distinction
paragraphs: Employees should understand the difference between:
list: Asking for clarification.
Raising a genuine operational concern.
Suggesting an alternative.
Refusing a reasonable instruction without justification.
Responding with insults or hostility.

sections.title: 9. Disagreeing with junior colleagues respectfully
paragraphs: Professional respect should not depend on job title.
A supervisor may disagree with an employee's suggestion without humiliating the employee.
A therapist suggests changing a room-preparation process.
The supervisor believes the existing arrangement is more suitable.
Poor response: "You don't have enough experience to tell us what to do."

Professional response: "Thank you for the suggestion. I understand why you think it could help. For now, we'll continue using the current procedure because it supports consistent preparation, but we can review your idea."
When employees are mocked for respectfully expressing ideas, they may stop raising useful concerns.
Authority should guide decisions, not silence respectful communication.

sections.title: 10. The difference between disagreement and being argumentative
paragraphs: Disagreement is not automatically argumentative behaviour.
An employee can disagree, explain her reasons and accept an appropriate decision.
Argumentative behaviour develops when someone repeatedly challenges others in an unproductive or hostile manner.
A receptionist suggests a different appointment arrangement.
The supervisor explains why it cannot be implemented.
Professional response: "Thank you for explaining. I understand the reason for the current arrangement."
Argumentative response: "No, you're wrong! I don't care what you say. My idea is better."
Persistently raising a serious safety concern, reporting misconduct or requesting a fair review should not automatically be labelled argumentative.
The nature of the concern and the manner of communication both matter.

sections.title: 11. How tone can turn disagreement into disrespect
paragraphs: Words are important, but tone also influences communication.
Consider the statement: "I don't agree with that."
It can be delivered calmly and respectfully.
It can also be delivered with contempt, ridicule or an aggressive tone.
Respectful: "I don't agree with that approach because I think it may delay the next client."
Disrespectful: "I don't agree with that! What kind of nonsense is this?"
The disagreement itself is not the problem.
The disrespectful language creates the problem.
You can be firm without being rude.
list: Speak at an appropriate volume.
Avoid shouting to overpower someone.
Do not use mocking laughter.
Avoid contemptuous facial expressions.
Allow the other person to finish.
Choose words that focus on the issue.

sections.title: 12. Setting boundaries is not automatically disrespectful
paragraphs: Employees should understand that saying "no" or setting an appropriate boundary is not automatically disrespectful.
A colleague repeatedly asks another employee to abandon her assigned responsibilities to complete unrelated tasks.
The employee responds: "I'm currently attending to my assigned duties, so I can't leave them right now. Please speak with the supervisor if the task needs to be reassigned."
This is a professional boundary.
An employee is being spoken to with insults.
She responds: "I'm willing to discuss the issue, but I would appreciate it if we could speak respectfully."
This is not automatically disrespectful.
It is a reasonable request for appropriate communication.
Respect does not require employees to agree to every request or tolerate abusive behaviour.

sections.title: 13. Disagreement during busy or stressful periods
paragraphs: Workplace pressure can make disagreements more difficult.
At Zura Spa, busy periods may involve multiple client arrivals, appointment changes, telephone enquiries, room preparation and unexpected operational issues.
A receptionist asks a therapist to prepare for an appointment earlier than expected.
The therapist believes the schedule does not allow enough preparation time.
Disrespectful response: "Stop disturbing me! Can't you see I'm busy?"
Professional response: "I understand the client is arriving earlier, but I need a few minutes to prepare the room properly. Can we confirm the timing with the client?"
The employee has expressed a concern without hostility.
Pressure may make respectful communication more difficult, but it does not make disrespect acceptable.

sections.title: 14. The AGREE method for respectful disagreement
paragraphs: Two employees disagree about when shared supplies should be checked.
One prefers checking everything at the beginning of the day.
The other believes supplies should be checked after every session.
Using AGREE, they acknowledge each other's reasoning, review the operational needs and suggest a combined approach.
They then confirm the appropriate procedure with the supervisor.
The goal is not to prove that one person is superior. The goal is to achieve the best practical outcome.

items.label: A — Acknowledge the other person's perspective
items.body: Show that you have heard and understood what the person is saying.

items.label: G — Give your perspective respectfully
items.body: Explain your opinion without insults, mockery or hostility.

items.label: R — Review the relevant facts
items.body: Consider available information rather than relying only on personal feelings.

items.label: E — Explore possible solutions
items.body: Look for an approach that addresses the concern and supports team objectives.

items.label: E — Establish the next step
items.body: Agree on an appropriate action or seek a decision from the responsible supervisor.

sections.title: 15. What to do when someone disagrees with you
paragraphs: Professionalism is not only about how you express disagreement.
It is also about how you respond when someone disagrees with you.
A therapist says: "I think the current handover process could be improved."
The colleague responds: "That's an interesting point. Which part do you think needs changing?"
This encourages constructive discussion.

items.label: 1. Listen before reacting.
items.body: Allow the person to explain their perspective.

items.label: 2. Avoid assuming disrespect.
items.body: A different opinion is not automatically an insult.

items.label: 3. Ask questions.
items.body: Seek clarification when the person's reasoning is unclear.

items.label: 4. Consider whether the person has a valid point.
items.body: You do not have to agree with everything, but you should remain open to useful information.

items.label: 5. Respond to the issue rather than attacking the person.
items.body: Explain your perspective calmly.

sections.title: 16. When disagreement becomes disrespectful
paragraphs: Sometimes a conversation begins respectfully but gradually becomes hostile.
"I think we're both becoming frustrated. Let's focus on the appointment issue and work out what needs to happen."
This response can help prevent escalation.
However, if the interaction involves threats, harassment or unsafe behaviour, employees should seek appropriate assistance rather than attempting to manage the situation alone.
list: Voices become increasingly aggressive.
Employees interrupt repeatedly.
Personal insults begin.
The original issue is forgotten.
Past grievances are introduced unnecessarily.
One person threatens or intimidates another.
Colleagues begin taking sides.
Someone deliberately mocks the other's opinion.

sections.title: What should employees do?
list: Recognise that the discussion is becoming unproductive.
Stop using accusatory or insulting language.
Refocus on the original issue.
Request a brief pause if necessary and appropriate.
Continue the discussion respectfully.
Involve the appropriate supervisor if the matter cannot be resolved.

sections.title: 17. Respect does not mean agreeing with everything
paragraphs: Some employees may believe that showing respect means remaining silent whenever they disagree.
This is not necessarily correct.
A supervisor instructs a therapist to begin a session before the treatment room has been properly prepared.
The therapist responds: "I understand the client is waiting, but the room isn't ready for use yet. I need to complete the required preparation before the session begins."
This is not automatically disrespectful.
The therapist is identifying a legitimate operational concern.
Respectful communication does not require abandoning good judgment.
list: Ask questions.
Seek clarification.
Suggest improvements.
Explain relevant facts.
Raise concerns about unfair treatment.
Report unsafe practices.
Set reasonable professional boundaries.

sections.title: 18. Practical case studies
paragraphs: Use the four case studies below in discussion. Identify the original issue, when communication became disrespectful, and what a professional response would look like.

sections.title: Case study A: The disagreement about room preparation
paragraphs: Two therapists disagree about the best time to replenish treatment-room supplies.
One suggests doing it immediately after each session.
The other suggests checking supplies before the next appointment.
The discussion becomes tense when one says: "Your suggestion is ridiculous."
Expected lesson: Different opinions can be discussed constructively without insults or personal attacks.
list: What was the original disagreement?
At what point did the communication become disrespectful?
How could the employee express her opinion differently?
What facts should the employees consider?
Who should confirm the appropriate procedure?

sections.title: Case study B: The receptionist and supervisor
paragraphs: A supervisor instructs a receptionist to change an appointment time.
The receptionist notices that the proposed time conflicts with another confirmed booking.
She respectfully raises the concern.
The supervisor responds: "Stop questioning me and just do what you're told."
Expected lesson: Respectful questions and factual concerns should not automatically be treated as challenges to authority.
list: Was the receptionist's question automatically disrespectful?
What operational concern did she identify?
How could the supervisor respond more professionally?
What should happen before the booking is changed?
Why is it important for employees to raise genuine concerns?

sections.title: Case study C: The employee who feels rejected
paragraphs: A therapist suggests a new way to organise supplies.
Her colleagues disagree and explain why the existing arrangement works better.
The therapist becomes offended and stops cooperating with them.
Expected lesson: Employees should not interpret every rejection of an idea as rejection of themselves.
list: Did the colleagues necessarily disrespect her?
Why might she feel rejected?
How could she respond more maturely?
Does disagreement mean her contribution has no value?
How can the team maintain cooperation?

sections.title: Case study D: The disrespectful disagreement
paragraphs: Two employees disagree about a shared responsibility.
One begins shouting and insulting the other.
The second employee responds with further insults.
The disagreement becomes a public argument.
Expected lesson: A disagreement becomes harmful when employees allow hostility and disrespect to replace constructive communication.
list: What was the original issue?
Which behaviours escalated the situation?
What could each employee have done differently?
When should a supervisor become involved?
How can the employees restore professional cooperation?

sections.title: 19. Practical group activity: Disagreement or disrespect?
paragraphs: Activity duration: 10 minutes.
Purpose: Help employees distinguish respectful disagreement from disrespectful communication.
The trainer should read each statement aloud. Participants should decide whether it represents respectful disagreement or disrespect.
Role-play: Divide participants into pairs. One person should present a suggestion about a workplace procedure. The other should disagree respectfully using the AGREE method. Then exchange roles.
Expected outcome: Employees practise expressing different opinions clearly without insults, hostility or unnecessary defensiveness.

items.label: 1. "I understand your suggestion, but I think another approach may work better."
items.body: Respectful disagreement.

items.label: 2. "Your idea is stupid. You clearly don't know what you're talking about."
items.body: Disrespect.

items.label: 3. "Could we review the appointment schedule? I think there may be a conflict."
items.body: Respectful disagreement.

items.label: 4. "Nobody asked for your opinion. Keep quiet."
items.body: Disrespect.

items.label: 5. "I see your point, but I don't agree with the proposed change."
items.body: Respectful disagreement.

items.label: 6. "Who do you think you are to question me?"
items.body: Disrespect.

sections.title: 20. Interactive assessment
paragraphs: Complete the Lesson 2 Knowledge Check at the bottom of this lesson. Choose an option, give your reason, then submit.
list: What is the main difference between disagreement and disrespect? Disagreement involves different opinions, while disrespect involves inappropriate treatment / Disagreement is always wrong, while disrespect is sometimes necessary / Disagreement only happens between supervisors
Which statement demonstrates respectful disagreement? Your idea is ridiculous. / I understand your point, but I see the situation differently. / Nobody asked for your opinion.

An employee respectfully questions a scheduling instruction because it conflicts with another booking. Is this automatically disrespectful? Yes, employees should never ask questions. / Yes, because disagreement always challenges authority. / No, raising a genuine operational concern respectfully can be appropriate.
What should you do when someone disagrees with your suggestion? Listen, consider their reasoning and respond respectfully / Immediately assume they dislike you / Refuse to cooperate with them

What does the AGREE method encourage? Arguing until everyone accepts your opinion / Acknowledging perspectives, giving your view, reviewing facts, exploring solutions and establishing next steps / Avoiding all discussions with colleagues

sections.title: 21. Personal assignment
paragraphs: Each employee should answer the following questions in writing.
list: Explain what disagreement means in the workplace.
Define disrespect and give five examples.
Identify five differences between disagreement and disrespect.
Explain why employees do not have to agree on everything to work successfully together.
Describe how a receptionist can respectfully disagree with a supervisor about an appointment arrangement.
Explain the difference between respectful disagreement and argumentative behaviour.
Describe how tone and choice of words can turn a disagreement into disrespect.
Explain why setting a reasonable professional boundary is not automatically disrespectful.
Describe the AGREE method in your own words.
Explain how you should respond when a colleague disagrees with your suggestion.
Identify three disrespectful communication habits you intend to avoid.
Describe one workplace disagreement and explain how it could be handled professionally.

sections.title: 22. Seven-day respectful disagreement challenge
table: Listen carefully when someone expresses a different opinion
Avoid interpreting disagreement as personal rejection
Practise disagreeing without insults or sarcasm
Ask clarifying questions instead of making assumptions
Use the AGREE method during a workplace discussion
Respectfully accept an appropriate decision even when your suggestion is not adopted
Reflect on how you can express disagreement while maintaining professional relationships

sections.title: 23. Final lesson and takeaway
paragraphs: Disagreement and disrespect are not the same.
Disagreement occurs when people have different opinions, ideas or perspectives.
Disrespect occurs when those differences are expressed through inappropriate or degrading behaviour.
At Zura Spa, employees should understand that they do not need to agree on every issue to maintain healthy professional relationships.
They should be willing to listen, explain their opinions, consider relevant facts and accept appropriate decisions.
Supervisors should also recognise that respectful questions, suggestions and concerns are not automatically challenges to their authority.
Next topic: Addressing Issues Instead of Attacking Personalities.

remember: You can disagree with someone without disrespecting them. You can reject an idea without rejecting the person who suggested it. You can express your opinion firmly without insulting others, and you can listen to a different perspective without losing your own voice. At Zura Spa, respect does not mean everyone must think alike. It means we value one another enough to communicate differences professionally, focus on what is right and work together toward the success of the team.
